items.stem: Students drop a course when they study very little and when they take on far too many other commitments. The students in the middle stay. Why can a single straight line not separate the stayers from the dropouts?

options.text: The stayers are in the middle with dropouts on both sides, and a line can only split the plot into two sides.
options.feedback: Whichever way you angle one line, some stayers end up on the same side as dropouts.

options.text: There are too few students to place a line.
options.feedback: The number of students is not the issue. The shape of the groups is.

options.text: The line has not been trained for long enough.
options.feedback: More training cannot fix a limit in the shape of a straight line.

options.text: Attendance matters more than hours studied.
options.feedback: Which measurement matters more does not change the fact that the stayers are surrounded.

items.stem: Before you try it: you switch off "Keep the nonlinearity" and move the Units slider from 1 up to 8. What do you expect to happen to the accuracy?

options.text: It does not improve. Adding straight lines together gives another straight line.
options.feedback: Without the nonlinearity, the layer can only add its units, and the sum of straight lines is a straight line. More units give no new shape.

options.text: It rises to 100 percent as units are added.
options.feedback: That happens only when the nonlinearity is on. Switched off, the units cannot combine into a curve.

options.text: It rises a little with each unit.
options.feedback: Each extra unit adds nothing new when the nonlinearity is off.
The network still draws a straight line, so some students are classified correctly.

items.try: Switch off "Keep the nonlinearity", move the Units slider from 1 to 8, and watch the Correct box.

items.stem: A neural network diagram for the dropout problem has four circles in the middle row. What does each circle correspond to on the plot?

options.text: One straight line, whose angle and position come from that unit's weights and bias
options.feedback: A unit is one line. Its two input weights set the angle and its bias sets how far out it sits.
Students are the points on the plot. The circles in the diagram are units.

options.text: One of the four regions where students stay
options.feedback: The stay region is the overlap of all the lines. It is not assigned to one unit.

options.text: One of the measurements a person chose to feed in
options.feedback: The measurements are the inputs on the left of the diagram. The middle circles are hidden units that the network sets up itself.

items.stem: A bank uses a deep learning model to score loan applications. The model is very accurate, but a regulator asks which measurements drove a particular rejection. Why is that hard to answer?

options.text: The model works out its own features inside its hidden layers, and no single number inside it has a plain meaning.
options.feedback: With hand-picked features you could point at the one that was wrong. In a deep network, billions of numbers combine and none of them means anything alone.

options.text: Deep learning models are always less accurate than simpler ones.
options.feedback: Deep models are often more accurate. The difficulty is explaining them.

options.text: The bank did not keep the applicant's data.
options.feedback: Having the data does not explain what the hidden layers did with it.

options.text: The output unit does not produce an answer.
options.feedback: The output unit does produce an answer. The hidden units that fed it are hard to interpret.
